historical_timeline.summary: The Supreme Court decides Hansberry v. Lee, the family's challenge to a restrictive covenant.
Her father dies suddenly in Mexico.
Marries Robert Nemiroff, three years after leaving Wisconsin for New York.
A Raisin in the Sun opens on Broadway, the first play by a Black woman produced there.
Fainting spells and attacks of nausea begin, first thought to be a duodenal ulcer.
After a collapse in pain and a ten-day admission in which cancer is diagnosed (she is told of anemia and bleeding ulcers), an unsuccessful operation in New York.
Surgery at the Lahey Clinic at the New England Baptist Hospital in Boston.
Gives the To Be Young, Gifted and Black speech on an afternoon out of hospital; The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window opens in October.
Dies of cancer at University Hospital in New York at 34.

claims.statement: Lorraine Vivian Hansberry was born in Chicago on May 19, 1930, the youngest of four children of Carl Augustus Hansberry, a successful real estate broker who founded one of the city's first Black banks, and Nannie Louise (Perry) Hansberry, a schoolteacher. Her grandfather had been born enslaved.

claims.statement: In 1937 her family moved into a house in the all-white Washington Park subdivision of Woodlawn in defiance of a racially restrictive covenant. The resulting case, Hansberry v. Lee, was decided in the family's favor by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1940.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern social history: a writer whose family fought housing segregation in court when she was a child.

claims.statement: She enrolled at the University of Wisconsin in 1948, left in 1950 for New York, and wrote for the newspaper Freedom. In June 1953 she married Robert Nemiroff. Sources differ on when they divorced (1962 or 1964); they continued to work together.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her working life as a writer anchors the modern social history; the marriage is recorded only as the sources state it.

claims.statement: A Raisin in the Sun opened at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre on Broadway on March 11, 1959, the first play by a Black woman to be produced on Broadway. It won the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award; she was the first Black playwright and, at 29, the youngest American to win it. In 1962 she moved to Croton-on-Hudson, New York.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her documented career anchors the modern social history: a playwright at work on her next play.

claims.statement: One account dates the start of her illness to April 1963, when she began to suffer from fainting spells and attacks of nausea; tests pointed at first to what was suspected to be a duodenal ulcer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern presenting problem (epigastric pain, nausea and near-fainting with iron deficiency anemia). The month comes from one reference work only.

claims.statement: In 1963 she had an attack, collapsed in pain and was in hospital for ten days, during which doctors diagnosed cancer; she was told she had anemia and bleeding ulcers.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented diagnosis to which the modern diagnosis is linked. That she was not told the diagnosis is the historical contrast with the modern episode, in which it is explained to her plainly. The month is not given.

claims.statement: She had an unsuccessful operation in New York in June 1963 and surgery at the Lahey Clinic at the New England Baptist Hospital in Boston in August 1963; one account dates the operations to June 24 and August 2, and neither cured the cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented surgery after the index date; the modern episode's operation is synthetic.

claims.statement: She kept writing and speaking through her illness. In May 1964, released from the hospital for the afternoon, she gave the speech that became known as To Be Young, Gifted and Black; in June she left her sickbed for a Town Hall debate; and in the fall she moved to a hotel near the rehearsals of The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window, attending its opening night in October 1964.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her documented wish to keep working anchors the modern plan built around her writing.

claims.statement: She died of cancer at University Hospital in New York on January 12, 1965, at 34; The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window closed that night. Her funeral was held in Harlem on January 15.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize pancreatic cancer in a young Black woman whose epigastric and back pain, weight loss, new diabetes and iron deficiency anemia could be put down to an ulcer or to stress, and care for it on the NCCN pancreatic adenocarcinoma guideline and the ASCO guidelines on potentially curable pancreatic cancer, palliative care and supportive care: pancreas-protocol CT and endoscopy at once; tissue by endoscopic ultrasound and biliary drainage before CA 19-9 is read; resectability staging and a multidisciplinary tumor board; germline genetic testing for every patient with pancreatic cancer and molecular profiling of the tumor; modified FOLFIRINOX before surgery for borderline resectable disease, with dose and support matched to her fitness; pancreaticoduodenectomy and chemotherapy after it; palliative care from the day of diagnosis; pain, nutrition and pancreatic enzyme replacement; diabetes caused by the pancreatic disease; venous thromboembolism risk; fertility and contraception; plain disclosure of the diagnosis and its prognosis; and a plan built around her wish to keep writing. Black Americans with pancreatic cancer are less often offered surgery and have worse survival, so each step is checked for delay.

visit_schedule.purpose: Two months of epigastric and back pain, weight loss, black stools and near-fainting in a woman of 32: examination, blood tests, and urgent upper endoscopy and pancreas-protocol CT
Diagnosis of pancreatic adenocarcinoma: tumor board plan, medical oncology consultation, genetic counseling, early palliative care, and planning of chemotherapy before surgery
Day 1 of cycle 4 of modified FOLFIRINOX: toxicity review, genetic and tumor profiling results, thromboprophylaxis, nutrition and mood
Same-day sick visit for diarrhea during chemotherapy
After six cycles: restaging CT and CA 19-9, decision for surgery, and preparation for pancreaticoduodenectomy
Six weeks after pancreaticoduodenectomy: pathology, diabetes and enzyme replacement after surgery, and the plan for chemotherapy after surgery
Periodic adult preventive visit during chemotherapy after surgery

hpi.narrative: Ms. Hansberry returns two weeks after her first visit. Upper endoscopy two days after that visit found no ulcer but an ulcerated mass in the duodenum next to the papilla, oozing slowly, and the biopsies show adenocarcinoma. The pancreas-protocol CT the next day showed a 3.1 cm mass in the head of the pancreas invading the duodenum, with dilated bile and pancreatic ducts and contact with more than half the circumference of the superior mesenteric vein, but no contact with the arteries and no spread to the liver, peritoneum or lungs. Endoscopic ultrasound a week ago confirmed pancreatic adenocarcinoma on biopsy, and a metal stent was placed in the bile duct at the same session; her urine is lighter and the itching has gone. The tumor board reviewed her five days ago. She had two doses of intravenous iron and has had no more black stools. Pain in the upper abdomen and back is 6 out of 10 and wakes her. Her stools are pale and float after fatty meals. She saw Dr. Adeyemi-Rourke this morning and genetic counseling this afternoon. She asked to be told everything plainly and was. She has had no thoughts of self-harm.

consultant_note.history: Ms. Hansberry, 32, is seen at the request of Dr. Marchetti-Fields two weeks after she presented with two months of epigastric and back pain, weight loss, black stools with iron deficiency anemia, and new diabetes. assessment.assessment: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the head of the pancreas invading the duodenum, which explains the bleeding, the anemia, the obstructed bile and pancreatic ducts, the pain and the new diabetes. By NCCN criteria it is borderline resectable, because the tumor contacts more than half the circumference of the superior mesenteric vein, although the vein can be reconstructed and no artery is involved; there is no distant spread on CT. For borderline resectable disease, chemotherapy first is preferred over going straight to surgery: it treats cancer that may already have spread unseen, can shrink the tumor away from the vein, and shows whether the cancer is controlled before a major operation. She is young and fit, with normal kidney function and bilirubin now normal, so modified FOLFIRINOX is the regimen of choice. The aim is cure, and surgery after chemotherapy offers the best chance of it; she was also told honestly that pancreatic cancer often returns even after successful surgery
